judgments.yea_description: Voted for Legislative Bill 89, which limits school and college sports teams by sex. Every covered team must be labeled for males, for females, or as coed. A team for females is closed to male students. A team for males is closed to female students, unless no female team is offered in that sport. To play on a team labeled by sex, a student must hand the school a paper signed by a doctor. It has to confirm the student's sex. The act defines male and female by the reproductive system a person naturally has, or would have had. It also shields a school that keeps separate teams for female students. No government body, licensing group or sports association may look into or punish such a school for keeping those teams. The rules cover public schools and colleges. They also cover private ones that play against them or belong to a sports association. The Nebraska Legislature passed it 33-16, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Legislative Bill 258, which slows future minimum wage increases and adds two lower wage rates. Nebraska's minimum wage reached fifteen dollars an hour in 2026. Under the law voters passed in 2022, it would then rise each year with the cost of living. That rise was tied to a federal price index. The act drops that link. From 2027 the wage goes up by a fixed one and three-quarters percent a year. The act also adds a youth minimum wage of thirteen dollars and fifty cents an hour. It covers workers who are at least fourteen, are under sixteen, and are not emancipated minors. That youth rate goes up one and one-half percent every fifth year, starting in 2030. The act rewrites the training wage too. An employer may pay that wage to a new worker for ninety days. It now covers new workers who are at least sixteen and under twenty. The act sets it at thirteen dollars and fifty cents an hour, rising one and one-half percent a year from 2027. Before the act, the training wage was seventy-five percent of the federal minimum wage. The Nebraska Legislature passed it 33-16, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Legislative Bill 266, which bars local governments from limiting rents. A city, village or county may not pass or enforce a local law that has the effect of rent control on private property. Any such law is void. The ban applies even where a city has its own home rule charter. Two things are still allowed. A local government may still use land-use rules or inclusionary housing rules that it adopts to add affordable housing. It may also run a program that a property owner joins by choice, under a contract that limits rent and rent increases. The Nebraska Legislature passed it 37-10, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Legislative Bill 966, which pays for school meals for students who now pay a reduced price. The act sets up the Hunger-Free Schools Pilot Program for the school years 2026-27 through 2031-32. A school may apply if it is already in the federal breakfast or lunch programs and does not already feed every student for free under the federal community eligibility option. The State Department of Education picks which of those schools take part. A school in the program serves breakfast or lunch at no cost to any student who qualifies for a reduced-price meal. It then reports how many of those meals it served. The state pays the school the gap between the federal payment for a free meal and the payment for a reduced-price meal. The act sets aside about 1.2 million dollars a year for the first two years. It replaces an older state payment of five cents for each school breakfast. The department must study how the program affects students and report by December 2032. The Nebraska Legislature passed it 38-11, and it became law.
